headline: Budget the characters unlike the majority
statement: Return the length of the longest contiguous substring that can be changed into all one letter using at most k replacements. s contains uppercase English letters.
intuition: For any continuous window, keep its most common letter and replace the others. The required number of replacements is the window length minus that letter's count. Extend the window, then shrink it if that cost exceeds k. Save the longest window that fits.
approach: Add the right character to a frequency map.
While window length minus the maximum frequency exceeds k, remove the left character and advance left.
Record the largest valid window length.
correctness: For a fixed window, replacing all non-majority letters is both sufficient and minimal. Extending right and removing left until this exact cost fits retains the longest valid window ending there: shrinking cannot make an invalid window larger and valid. Maximizing over endpoints finds the best possible result.
bruteForce: Examine every substring and count its majority letter, costing O(n²) windows and repeated work.

complexity.explanation: Both boundaries move forward only; finding a maximum scans at most 26 character counts.

pitfalls: Replacement cost is not the number of distinct letters.
Removing a character can lower the exact majority count.
k is an upper bound, so fewer replacements are allowed.
